[[:db/retract 17592186118334 :answer-field/choices 17592186118336] {:db/id 17592186119763 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-41bae79a-9c3e-5b74-b3cc-213f841b749e" "question-8a0a2c2f-1706-5f21-a00b-714f5830e8bd" "question-62dfa070-b095-529f-9742-123438c631da"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119761 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119762 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-41bae79a-9c3e-5b74-b3cc-213f841b749e" :question/id #uuid "41bae79a-9c3e-5b74-b3cc-213f841b749e" :question/math-academy-id "q-162415" :question/problem "The curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{1}{t+1}\,j$ is given by 

$$
κ(t)=\frac{2(t+1)^{3}}{\bbox[2pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAA}}},\,t>-1.
$$

 
What is the missing part of the expression?" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=\frac{1}{t+1}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =\frac{2}{(t+1)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|1\cdot \frac{2}{(t+1)^{3}}-0\cdot (-\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}})|}{{({1}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}})}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\frac{2}{(t+1)^{3}}|}{{(1+\frac{1}{(t+1)^{4}})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\frac{2}{(t+1)^{3}}|}{\sqrt{{[\frac{(t+1)^{4}+1}{(t+1)^{4}}]}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{2(t+1)^{6}}{|(t+1)^{3}|\sqrt{{((t+1)^{4}+1)}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{2(t+1)^{6}}{(t+1)^{3}\sqrt{{((t+1)^{4}+1)}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{2(t+1)^{3}}{\sqrt{{((t+1)^{4}+1)}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we removed the absolute value because $t>-1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-227607dc-c995-56fe-a20c-664bdc03dd83"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-227607dc-c995-56fe-a20c-664bdc03dd83" :answer-field/id #uuid "227607dc-c995-56fe-a20c-664bdc03dd83" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-514f5bcf-ca33-5ef0-a733-ec86dffae285" :answer-field/choices ["answer-da852d6f-b131-56d4-8256-fdebdbc61a5a" "answer-8538bef5-2a64-541e-8605-5f22bd698faa" "answer-b649dd5a-85ff-5b4b-adbd-8d96f4510c5a" "answer-514f5bcf-ca33-5ef0-a733-ec86dffae285"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-da852d6f-b131-56d4-8256-fdebdbc61a5a" :answer/id #uuid "da852d6f-b131-56d4-8256-fdebdbc61a5a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{(t+1)^{2}+1}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8538bef5-2a64-541e-8605-5f22bd698faa" :answer/id #uuid "8538bef5-2a64-541e-8605-5f22bd698faa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{(t+1)^{3}+1}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b649dd5a-85ff-5b4b-adbd-8d96f4510c5a" :answer/id #uuid "b649dd5a-85ff-5b4b-adbd-8d96f4510c5a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{{((t+1)^{2}+1)}^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-514f5bcf-ca33-5ef0-a733-ec86dffae285" :answer/id #uuid "514f5bcf-ca33-5ef0-a733-ec86dffae285" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{{((t+1)^{4}+1)}^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281461 :question/problem "The curvature of the plane curve $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+2t\,j$ is given by 

$$
κ(t)=\frac{2{e}^{t}}{\bbox[2pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAA}}}.
$$

 
What is the missing part of the expression?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-8a0a2c2f-1706-5f21-a00b-714f5830e8bd" :question/id #uuid "8a0a2c2f-1706-5f21-a00b-714f5830e8bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-162419" :question/problem "The signed curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=⟨1-2t,\,{e}^{2t}⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{\bbox[2pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}}{\sqrt{(1+{e}^{4t})^{3}}}.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?" :question/worked-solution "The signed curvature $k(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t)⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=1-2t,\,y(t)={e}^{2t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-2,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =2{e}^{2t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =4{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{-2\cdot 4{e}^{2t}-0\cdot 2{e}^{2t}}{{((-2)^{2}+(2{e}^{2t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-8{e}^{2t}}{{(4+4{e}^{4t})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-8{e}^{2t}}{8{(1+{e}^{4t})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-{e}^{2t}}{\sqrt{(1+{e}^{4t})^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-13db80f1-1ccc-58f1-8641-3684ab9f70ba"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-13db80f1-1ccc-58f1-8641-3684ab9f70ba" :answer-field/id #uuid "13db80f1-1ccc-58f1-8641-3684ab9f70ba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-16c29e5d-b1a7-5613-96fd-eb90123329c2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-18321e2d-03ab-5b7f-b6cf-eb257b7975d8" "answer-16c29e5d-b1a7-5613-96fd-eb90123329c2" "answer-7dd01b5f-502e-5b84-8ab6-aef88da96da0" "answer-76ff0fbe-7e33-5c49-a981-0cf35543aabc" "answer-8fab1247-6445-5427-bfd4-c38eeb5e52b8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-18321e2d-03ab-5b7f-b6cf-eb257b7975d8" :answer/id #uuid "18321e2d-03ab-5b7f-b6cf-eb257b7975d8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2{e}^{2t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-16c29e5d-b1a7-5613-96fd-eb90123329c2" :answer/id #uuid "16c29e5d-b1a7-5613-96fd-eb90123329c2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{e}^{2t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7dd01b5f-502e-5b84-8ab6-aef88da96da0" :answer/id #uuid "7dd01b5f-502e-5b84-8ab6-aef88da96da0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{e}^{2t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76ff0fbe-7e33-5c49-a981-0cf35543aabc" :answer/id #uuid "76ff0fbe-7e33-5c49-a981-0cf35543aabc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{2t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8fab1247-6445-5427-bfd4-c38eeb5e52b8" :answer/id #uuid "8fab1247-6445-5427-bfd4-c38eeb5e52b8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{4t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-62dfa070-b095-529f-9742-123438c631da" :question/id #uuid "62dfa070-b095-529f-9742-123438c631da" :question/math-academy-id "q-162416" :question/problem "The signed curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t}⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{2}{\bbox[2pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAA}}}.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?" :question/worked-solution "The signed curvature $k(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t)⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{t},\,y(t)={e}^{-t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t},\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-{e}^{-t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t},\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-(-{e}^{-t})\cdot {e}^{t}}{{(({e}^{t})^{2}+({e}^{-t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{{({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t})^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d781f999-1594-5949-8737-c9a323ba0c9c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d781f999-1594-5949-8737-c9a323ba0c9c" :answer-field/id #uuid "d781f999-1594-5949-8737-c9a323ba0c9c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3478a58b-9f79-5e34-a211-77269420ac07" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3478a58b-9f79-5e34-a211-77269420ac07" "answer-b42b656a-892d-51db-80a8-a81810a225fa" "answer-4d339910-47cb-5c30-93e5-6488d858b18e" "answer-a4a98d71-c58f-5d5f-a189-b5539ed24ce8" "answer-037e0218-2ccb-5fc5-a7d9-90d6fd723b88"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3478a58b-9f79-5e34-a211-77269420ac07" :answer/id #uuid "3478a58b-9f79-5e34-a211-77269420ac07" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t})^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b42b656a-892d-51db-80a8-a81810a225fa" :answer/id #uuid "b42b656a-892d-51db-80a8-a81810a225fa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{({e}^{t}+{e}^{-t})^{3}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4d339910-47cb-5c30-93e5-6488d858b18e" :answer/id #uuid "4d339910-47cb-5c30-93e5-6488d858b18e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2{e}^{t}+2{e}^{-t}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a4a98d71-c58f-5d5f-a189-b5539ed24ce8" :answer/id #uuid "a4a98d71-c58f-5d5f-a189-b5539ed24ce8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-037e0218-2ccb-5fc5-a7d9-90d6fd723b88" :answer/id #uuid "037e0218-2ccb-5fc5-a7d9-90d6fd723b88" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{{e}^{t}+{e}^{-t}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186401350 :question/problem "The signed curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-{t}^{2}⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{2\cdot (\,\bbox[2pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}\,)}{\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})^{3}}}.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a" :question/id #uuid "37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-162422" :question/problem "Find the radius of the curvature for the curve $r(t)=⟨(1-t)^{2},\,{e}^{t}⟩$ at $t=0.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=(1-t)^{2},\,y(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-2(1-t),\, & {y}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|-2(1-t)\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 2|}{({(-2(1-t))^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|2t{e}^{t}-4{e}^{t}|}{({(2(1-t))^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{|2(0){e}^{(0)}-4{e}^{(0)}|}{({(2(1-(0)))^{2}+({e}^{(0)})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{5}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0dbf3265-830d-57eb-a3a8-4ed3e1aae9cd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0dbf3265-830d-57eb-a3a8-4ed3e1aae9cd" :answer-field/id #uuid "0dbf3265-830d-57eb-a3a8-4ed3e1aae9cd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0c476023-3edd-5454-ad4c-d620372551a6" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c9d40450-bdc6-5d3a-b702-e8236d07b93e" "answer-0c476023-3edd-5454-ad4c-d620372551a6" "answer-5b451fb0-b40b-5c70-b25e-e6d23ad872c3" "answer-f0de606c-6689-5321-a410-2a40373d9b5e" "answer-d8b8ff58-1e96-5cc3-b54c-7bc562e920f3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c9d40450-bdc6-5d3a-b702-e8236d07b93e" :answer/id #uuid "c9d40450-bdc6-5d3a-b702-e8236d07b93e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\sqrt{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0c476023-3edd-5454-ad4c-d620372551a6" :answer/id #uuid "0c476023-3edd-5454-ad4c-d620372551a6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5b451fb0-b40b-5c70-b25e-e6d23ad872c3" :answer/id #uuid "5b451fb0-b40b-5c70-b25e-e6d23ad872c3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f0de606c-6689-5321-a410-2a40373d9b5e" :answer/id #uuid "f0de606c-6689-5321-a410-2a40373d9b5e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d8b8ff58-1e96-5cc3-b54c-7bc562e920f3" :answer/id #uuid "d8b8ff58-1e96-5cc3-b54c-7bc562e920f3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120370 :question/problem "Find the radius of curvature for the curve $r(t)=(1-t)\,i+{e}^{t}\,j$ at $t=0.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=1-t,\,y(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot {e}^{t}-({e}^{t})\cdot 0|}{{((-1)^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{{(1+{e}^{2t})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{{e}^{0}}{{(1+{e}^{2(0)})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(1+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186118334 :answer-field/correct 17592186118335 :answer-field/choices ["answer-bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35" :answer/id #uuid "bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{(1+e)^{3/2}}{e}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647" :question/id #uuid "0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647" :question/math-academy-id "q-162524" :question/problem "Find the curvature of the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ at $x=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
κ(x)=\frac{|{y}^{″}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\, & {y}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|-\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x|}{{[1+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2}]}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{|-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi |}{{[1+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|1-0|}{{[1+(0+1)^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t), \: y(t) \rangle,
$$

the *curvature* of $C$ at an arbitrary point can be found using the following formula:

$$
\kappa(t)  = \dfrac{|x'(t)y''(t) - y'(t)x''(t)|}{ (x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}
$$

Additionally, the **signed curvature** $k$ is given by

$$
k(t) = \dfrac{x'(t)y''(t) - y'(t)x''(t)}{ (x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}.
$$

For example, consider a curve defined by the parametric equations

$$
x(t) = 2t, \qquad
y(t) = 1+t^2.
$$

Let's find the curvature of this curve at the point where $t=1.$

First, we calculate the first and second derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{′}(t)=2,\, & {y}^{′}(t)=2t \\  & {x}^{″}(t)=0,\, & {y}^{″}(t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these expressions into our curvature formula, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2\cdot 2-2t\cdot 0|}{{[{2}^{2}+(2t)^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\,4\,|}{{2}^{3}{[1+{t}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{({t}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t =1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{1}{2{({1}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121013 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a plane curve defined by the explicit equation 

$$
y = y(x).
$$

In this case, we can parametrize this curve as follows:

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle t, \: y(t) \rangle.
$$

Now, using the fact that $x=t,$ we calculate the first and second derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′}(x) \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={y}^{″}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the (unsigned) curvature, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|1\cdot {y}^{″}(x)-{y}^{′}(x)\cdot 0|}{({1}^{2}+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|{y}^{″}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unsigned curvature for $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
\kappa (x) = \dfrac{|y''(x)|}{ (1 + [y'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}
$$

and the signed curvature is

$$
k(x) = \dfrac {y''(x)} {(1+[y'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}	.
$$

Note that the signed curvature $k(x)$ has the same sign as $y''(x).$ Therefore,

- if $k(x) > 0,$ the curve is concave up, and

- if $k(x) < 0,$ the curve is concave down." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121012 :tutorial/content "We've been using the following formula for unsigned curvature:

$$
\kappa (t)  = \dfrac{|x'(t)y''(t) - y'(t)x''(t)|}{ (x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}
$$

To see where this formula comes from, remember that for a curve $\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),  y(t),  z(t)\rangle,$ the unsigned curvature formula is

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}.
$$

If a curve does not have a $z$-component, then we may consider $z(t) = 0.$ Thus, any plane curve $\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t), \: y(t) \rangle$ can be represented as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t), \:  y(t), \: 0\rangle.
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r''(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf r'(t) = \langle x'(t), y'(t),0 \rangle, \qquad \mathbf r''(t) = \langle x''(t), y''(y),0 \rangle
$$

Substituting these expressions into our cross-product formula, we find that the curvature $\kappa(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{‖⟨{x}^{′}(t),{y}^{′}(t),0⟩\times ⟨{x}^{″}(t),{y}^{″}(t),0⟩‖}{‖⟨{x}^{′}(t),{y}^{′}(t)⟩{‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{‖⟨0,0,{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)⟩‖}{(\sqrt{{x}^{′}(t)^{2}+{y}^{′}(t)^{2}})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{({x}^{′}(t)^{2}+{y}^{′}(t)^{2})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120038 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

What is the missing part of the expression?" :question/worked-solution "The signed curvature $k(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t)⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{t},\,y(t)={e}^{-t}.

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t},\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-{e}^{-t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t},\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}

$$

What is the missing part of the expression?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a" :question/id #uuid "37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-162422" :question/problem "Find the radius of the curvature for the curve $r(t)=⟨(1-t)^{2},\,{e}^{t}⟩$ at $t=0.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=(1-t)^{2},\,y(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-2(1-t),\, & {y}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|-2(1-t)\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 2|}{({(-2(1-t))^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|2t{e}^{t}-4{e}^{t}|}{({(2(1-t))^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{|2(0){e}^{(0)}-4{e}^{(0)}|}{({(2(1-(0)))^{2}+({e}^{(0)})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{5}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=1-t,\,y(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot {e}^{t}-({e}^{t})\cdot 0|}{{((-1)^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{{(1+{e}^{2t})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{{e}^{0}}{{(1+{e}^{2(0)})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(1+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186118334 :answer-field/correct 17592186118335 :answer-field/choices ["answer-bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35" :answer/id #uuid "bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{(1+e)^{3/2}}{e}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647" :question/id #uuid "0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647" :question/math-academy-id "q-162524" :question/problem "Find the curvature of the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ at $x=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
κ(x)=\frac{|{y}^{″}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\, & {y}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|-\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x|}{{[1+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2}]}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{|-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi |}{{[1+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|1-0|}{{[1+(0+1)^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b69e114a-e3b9-5a0f-8073-62abdcb55456"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b69e114a-e3b9-5a0f-8073-62abdcb55456" :answer-field/id #uuid "b69e114a-e3b9-5a0f-8073-62abdcb55456" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e634d627-dd7c-5af7-b31a-020ab478d655" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8b8c1238-64a6-5834-b740-28291402e0cf" "answer-af28de7d-ae99-5116-bc25-465dc14a4553" "answer-6d9ba14f-0d41-5eb4-ad9c-a3ca3c24f04a" "answer-9bd14e87-92c1-5247-b76f-922de0ae6d11" "answer-e634d627-dd7c-5af7-b31a-020ab478d655"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8b8c1238-64a6-5834-b740-28291402e0cf" :answer/id #uuid "8b8c1238-64a6-5834-b740-28291402e0cf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-af28de7d-ae99-5116-bc25-465dc14a4553" :answer/id #uuid "af28de7d-ae99-5116-bc25-465dc14a4553" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6d9ba14f-0d41-5eb4-ad9c-a3ca3c24f04a" :answer/id #uuid "6d9ba14f-0d41-5eb4-ad9c-a3ca3c24f04a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9bd14e87-92c1-5247-b76f-922de0ae6d11" :answer/id #uuid "9bd14e87-92c1-5247-b76f-922de0ae6d11" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e634d627-dd7c-5af7-b31a-020ab478d655" :answer/id #uuid "e634d627-dd7c-5af7-b31a-020ab478d655" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121011 :tutorial/content "For a plane curve $C$ defined by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t), \: y(t) \rangle,
$$

the *curvature* of $C$ at an arbitrary point can be found using the following formula:

$$
\kappa(t)  = \dfrac{|x'(t)y''(t) - y'(t)x''(t)|}{ (x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}
$$

Additionally, the **signed curvature** $k$ is given by

$$
k(t) = \dfrac{x'(t)y''(t) - y'(t)x''(t)}{ (x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}.
$$

For example, consider a curve defined by the parametric equations

$$
x(t) = 2t, \qquad
y(t) = 1+t^2.
$$

Let's find the curvature of this curve at the point where $t=1.$

First, we calculate the first and second derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{′}(t)=2,\, & {y}^{′}(t)=2t \\  & {x}^{″}(t)=0,\, & {y}^{″}(t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these expressions into our curvature formula, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2\cdot 2-2t\cdot 0|}{{[{2}^{2}+(2t)^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\,4\,|}{{2}^{3}{[1+{t}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{({t}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t =1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{1}{2{({1}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121013 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a plane curve defined by the explicit equation 

$$

In this case, we can parametrize this curve as follows:

Now, using the fact that $x=t,$ we calculate the first and second derivatives of the components:

\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′}(x) \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={y}^{″}(x)\end{aligned}

Substituting these into the formula for the (unsigned) curvature, we get

$$

Therefore, the unsigned curvature for $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$

Note that the signed curvature $k(x)$ has the same sign as $y''(x).$ Therefore,

- if $k(x) > 0,$ the curve is concave up, and

- if $k(x) < 0,$ the curve is concave down." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121012 :tutorial/content "We've been using the following formula for unsigned curvature:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t},\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-{e}^{-t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t},\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-(-{e}^{-t})\cdot {e}^{t}}{{(({e}^{t})^{2}+({e}^{-t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{{({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t})^{3}}}\end{aligned}

What is the missing part of the expression?"] ["question-37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a" :question/id #uuid "37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a"] ["question-37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-162422"] ["question-37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a" :question/problem "Find the radius of the curvature for the curve $r(t)=⟨(1-t)^{2},\,{e}^{t}⟩$ at $t=0.$"] ["question-37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=(1-t)^{2},\,y(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-2(1-t),\, & {y}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|-2(1-t)\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 2|}{({(-2(1-t))^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|2t{e}^{t}-4{e}^{t}|}{({(2(1-t))^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{|2(0){e}^{(0)}-4{e}^{(0)}|}{({(2(1-(0)))^{2}+({e}^{(0)})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{5}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-37e058b7-fa62-5f7d-a443-fba67e4c6b5a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0dbf3265-830d-57eb-a3a8-4ed3e1aae9cd" :answer-field/id #uuid curvature for the curve $r(t)=(1-t)\,i+{e}^{t}\,j$ at $t=0.$"] [17592186120370 :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=1-t,\,y(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot {e}^{t}-({e}^{t})\cdot 0|}{{((-1)^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{{(1+{e}^{2t})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{{e}^{0}}{{(1+{e}^{2(0)})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(1+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186120370 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35" :answer/id #uuid "bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35"] ["answer-bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35" :answer/value "\frac{(1+e)^{3/2}}{e}"] [17592186118334 :answer-field/correct 17592186118335] [17592186118334 :answer-field/choices "answer-bc367fc5-9c04-507f-a154-cf7c0d7dcc35"] ["question-0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647" :question/id #uuid "0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647"] ["question-0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647" :question/math-academy-id "q-162524"] ["question-0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647" :question/problem "Find the curvature of the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ at $x=\pi .$"] ["question-0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
κ(x)=\frac{|{y}^{″}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\, & {y}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|-\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x|}{{[1+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2}]}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{|-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi |}{{[1+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|1-0|}{{[1+(0+1)^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0e3e184e-e905-5d9a-a39c-5d0db9ad9647" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b69e114a-e3b9-5a0f-8073-62abdcb55456" :answer-field/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the radius of the curvature for the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{3},\,1-t⟩$ at $t=1.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)={t}^{3},\,y(t)=1-t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =3{t}^{2},\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =6t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|3{t}^{2}\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot 6t|}{{((3t)^{2}+(1)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6|t|}{{(9{t}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{6|1|}{{(9(1)^{2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{(10)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{5\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(1) & =\frac{1}{κ(1)}=\frac{5\sqrt{10}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281468 :question/id #uuid "9bbbf354-282e-5ba3-92a4-09b0417fb35b" :question/math-academy-id "q-162403"} {:db/id 17592186281469 :question/id #uuid $R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)={t}^{2}-1,\,y(t)=1-t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =2t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2t\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot 2|}{{((2t)^{2}+(-1)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(4{t}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\frac{1}{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\frac{1}{2}) & =\frac{2}{{(4{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(1+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{1}{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{1}{2}) & =\frac{1}{κ(\frac{1}{2})}=\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))|}{{((2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|-8{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-8{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)|}{{(4{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t))}^{3/2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =1\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{κ(\frac{\pi }{2})}=1.\end{aligned}

$$
\kappa(x) = \dfrac {|y''(x)|} {(1+[y'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate $y'(x)$ and $y''(x){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2},\, & {y}^{″}(x) & =6x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|6x|}{{[1+{(3{x}^{2})}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|6x|}{{(1+9{x}^{4})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(-1) & =\frac{|6(-1)|}{{(1+9(-1)^{4})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|-6|}{{(1+9)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{10}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{10\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{50}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120347 :question/id #uuid "08113b99-b301-5e33-b007-837ba481f7b5" :question/math-academy-id "q-34549" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119762 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "384072a8-f008-5279-bb58-8086eb42b710" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Cartesian Form"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04645806-e767-51f6-b56b-a967a3dc35eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{25}" :db/id 17592186317584} {:answer/id #uuid "16fca06f-ad2b-5ab8-8589-6844750db1b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}" :db/id 17592186317638} {:answer/id #uuid "815819ce-d705-5379-ba5c-0d922afcf192" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186318002} {:answer/id #uuid "8bad3fd1-ca56-5eea-b1ef-c4edb5db52bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{27}" :db/id 17592186318034} {:answer/id #uuid "8f73c15c-c406-513b-871a-da9696850ca1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}" :db/id 17592186318054}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "04645806-e767-51f6-b56b-a967a3dc35eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{25}" :db/id 17592186317584} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6368194-6360-5320-9e2f-ba4aa8d2e3e8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186318908}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the curvature of the curve $y=2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)$ at $x=2.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}-4x,\, & {y}^{″}(x) & =6x-4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|6x-4|}{{[1+{(3{x}^{2}-4x)}^{2}]}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=-1$ is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,{y}^{″}(x)={2}^{x}{ln}^{2}⁡2

$$
\begin{aligned}k(x) & =\frac{{2}^{x}{ln}^{2}⁡2}{{[1+{({2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{x}{ln}^{2}⁡2}{{(1+{2}^{2x}{ln}^{2}⁡2)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}k(-1) & =\frac{{2}^{-1}{ln}^{2}⁡2}{{(1+{2}^{2(-1)}{ln}^{2}⁡2)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡2}{2})}{{(\frac{4+{ln}^{2}⁡2}{4})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4{ln}^{2}⁡2}{(4+{ln}^{2}⁡2)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}

$$
k (t) = \dfrac {x'(t) y''(t) - y'(t) x''(t)} {\big([x'(t)]^2 + [y'(t)]^2\big)^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad y(t) = \sin t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{({1}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\sqrt{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡t)^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048648} {:db/id 17592186120345 :question/id #uuid "ddcaea90-80a7-5b60-9d82-b87ebbb01019" :question/math-academy-id "q-34544"} {:db/id 17592186120378 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186120601 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121011 :tutorial/content "For a plane curve $C$ defined by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t), \: y(t) \rangle,
$$

the *curvature* of $C$ at an arbitrary point can be found using the following formula:

$$
\kappa(t)  = \dfrac{|x'(t)y''(t) - y'(t)x''(t)|}{ (x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}
$$

Additionally, the **signed curvature** $k$ is given by

$$
k(t) = \dfrac{x'(t)y''(t) - y'(t)x''(t)}{ (x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}.
$$

The signed curvature tells us whether the curve bends up, down, or straight:

* if [math]k > 0,[/math] then the curve bends upward (i.e., it is concave up)

* if [math]k < 0,[/math] then the curve bends downward (i.e., it is concave up)

* if [math]k=0,[/math] then the curve is straight.

For example, consider a curve defined by the parametric equations

$$
x(t) = 2t, \qquad
y(t) = 1+t^2.
$$

Let's find the curvature of this curve at the point where $t=1.$

First, we calculate the first and second derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{'}(t)=2,\, & {y}^{'}(t)=2t \\  & {x}^{''}(t)=0,\, & {y}^{''}(t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these expressions into our curvature formula, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2\cdot 2-2t\cdot 0|}{{[{2}^{2}+(2t)^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\,4\,|}{{2}^{3}{[1+{t}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{({t}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t =1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{1}{2{({1}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b40dd6c7-fe0a-5126-9014-ec7c0d5eb29b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2534 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "402c2124-8063-56c7-bb37-ea2cdcc0a66c" :step/math-academy-id 11439 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120606}} {:db/id 17592186120602 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119761 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119577 :question/id #uuid "1f374865-c7f7-510c-b361-fbad352d86c6" :question/math-academy-id "e-3452"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "36986a18-172c-5983-8f6f-3211b6e8f89d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048339}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120370} {:db/id 17592186120499} {:db/id 17592186281465} {:db/id 17592186281468} {:db/id 17592186281469} {:db/id 17592186281470} {:db/id 17592186281473} {:db/id 17592186281474} {:db/id 17592186281477}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Radius of Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Parametric Form"} :step/id #uuid "71cffa1e-47f4-55d9-a319-71cf51f73286" :step/math-academy-id 11440 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120604}} {:db/id 17592186120603 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121012 :tutorial/content "We've been using the following formula for unsigned curvature:

$$
\kappa (t)  = \dfrac{|x'(t)y''(t) - y'(t)x''(t)|}{ (x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}
$$

To see where this formula comes from, remember that for a curve $\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),  y(t),  z(t)\rangle,$ the unsigned curvature formula is

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}.
$$

If a curve does not have a $z$-component, then we may consider $z(t) = 0.$ Thus, any plane curve $\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t), \: y(t) \rangle$ can be represented as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t), \:  y(t), \: 0\rangle.
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r''(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf r'(t) = \langle x'(t), y'(t),0 \rangle, \qquad \mathbf r''(t) = \langle x''(t), y''(y),0 \rangle
$$

Substituting these expressions into our cross-product formula, we find that the curvature $\kappa(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{‖⟨{x}^{'}(t),{y}^{'}(t),0⟩\times ⟨{x}^{''}(t),{y}^{''}(t),0⟩‖}{‖⟨{x}^{'}(t),{y}^{'}(t)⟩{‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{‖⟨0,0,{x}^{'}(t){y}^{''}(t)-{y}^{'}(t){x}^{''}(t)⟩‖}{(\sqrt{{x}^{'}(t)^{2}+{y}^{'}(t)^{2}})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{|{x}^{'}(t){y}^{''}(t)-{y}^{'}(t){x}^{''}(t)|}{({x}^{'}(t)^{2}+{y}^{'}(t)^{2})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "16d4e0f1-81e9-5252-9390-52f2e8512d48" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2535 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula for the Curvature of a Plane Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "f6ca150c-baf4-5085-bb7d-62a05a15bc30" :step/math-academy-id 11441} {:db/id 17592186120604 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121013 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a plane curve defined by the explicit equation 

$$
y = y(x).
$$

In this case, we can parametrize this curve as follows:

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle t, \: y(t) \rangle.
$$

Now, using the fact that $x=t,$ we calculate the first and second derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{'}(t) & ={y}^{'}(x) \\ {x}^{''}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{''}(t) & ={y}^{''}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the (unsigned) curvature, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|{x}^{'}(t){y}^{''}(t)-{y}^{'}(t){x}^{''}(t)|}{([{x}^{'}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{'}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|1\cdot {y}^{''}(x)-{y}^{'}(x)\cdot 0|}{({1}^{2}+[{y}^{'}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|{y}^{''}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{'}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unsigned curvature for $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
\kappa (x) = \dfrac{|y''(x)|}{ (1 + [y'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}
$$

and the signed curvature is

$$
k(x) = \dfrac {y''(x)} {(1+[y'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}	.
$$

Note that the signed curvature $k(x)$ has the same sign as $y''(x).$ Therefore,

- if $k(x) > 0,$ the curve is concave up, and

- if $k(x) < 0,$ the curve is concave down." :tutorial/id #uuid "66d1756a-304e-51f3-9622-3074a6e63c70" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2536 :tutorial/title "The Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Cartesian \mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t), \:  y(t), \: 0\rangle.
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r''(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf r'(t) = \langle x'(t), y'(t),0 \rangle, \qquad \mathbf r''(t) = \langle x''(t), y''(y),0 \rangle
$$

Substituting these expressions into our cross-product formula, we find that the curvature $\kappa(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{'}(t)\times {r}^{''}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{'}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{‖⟨{x}^{'}(t),{y}^{'}(t),0⟩\times ⟨{x}^{''}(t),{y}^{''}(t),0⟩‖}{‖⟨{x}^{'}(t),{y}^{'}(t)⟩{‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{‖⟨0,0,{x}^{'}(t){y}^{''}(t)-{y}^{'}(t){x}^{''}(t)⟩‖}{(\sqrt{{x}^{'}(t)^{2}+{y}^{'}(t)^{2}})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{|{x}^{'}(t){y}^{''}(t)-{y}^{'}(t){x}^{''}(t)|}{({x}^{'}(t)^{2}+{y}^{'}(t)^{2})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "16d4e0f1-81e9-5252-9390-52f2e8512d48" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2535 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula for the Curvature of a Plane Parametric Curve"} {:db/id 17592186121013 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a plane curve defined by the explicit equation 

$$
y = y(x).
$$

In this case, we can parametrize this curve as follows:

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle t, \: y(t) \rangle.
$$

Now, using the fact that $x=t,$ we calculate the first and second derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{'}(t) & ={y}^{'}(x) \\ {x}^{''}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{''}(t) & ={y}^{''}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the (unsigned) curvature, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|{x}^{'}(t){y}^{''}(t)-{y}^{'}(t){x}^{''}(t)|}{([{x}^{'}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{'}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|1\cdot {y}^{''}(x)-{y}^{'}(x)\cdot 0|}{({1}^{2}+[{y}^{'}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|{y}^{''}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{'}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unsigned curvature for $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
\kappa (x) = \dfrac{|y''(x)|}{ (1 + [y'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}
$$

and the signed curvature is

$$
k(x) = \dfrac {y''(x)} {(1+[y'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}	.
$$

Note that the signed curvature $k(x)$ has the same sign as $y''(x).$ Therefore,

- if $k(x) > 0,$ the curve is concave up, and

- if $k(x) < 0,$ the curve is concave down." :tutorial/id #uuid "66d1756a-304e-51f3-9622-3074a6e63c70" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2536 :tutorial/title "The Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Cartesian Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating 17592186045417] [17592186119577 1074 "The curvature $\kappa(t)$ of a plane curve $\mathbf r(t) = x(t) \, \mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j$ is given by

$$
\kappa (t) = \dfrac {|x'(t) y''(t) - y'(t) x''(t)|} {\big([x'(t)]^2 + [y'(t)]^2\big)^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad y(t) = \sin t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 0|}{{({1}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}⁡t|}{{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t = \dfrac{\pi}2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})|}{{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(1+{0}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t = \dfrac{\pi}2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{κ(\frac{\pi }{2})}=1.\end{aligned}
$$" 17592186045417] [17592186119578 1069 "e-3453" 17592186045417] [17592186119578 1071 "Find the curvature of the curve $y = x^3$ at $x=-1.$" 17592186045417] [17592186119578 1072 #uuid "2ff129e7-a923-5510-a35b-a6be403152ac" 17592186045417] [17592186119578 1074 "The curvature $\kappa(x)$ of a plane curve $y = y(x)$ is given by
